generated_by: prism-parity:tools/generate-browser-refusals.php for php; the ports' own runners for ts and py. The CODE is the contract and is pinned; the sentence is not, and is deliberately never pinned — the three implementations word these differently on purpose, and a test over the prose holds every language to a translation.

cases.title: an allowed host on https
cases.notes: The control. Every other row in this suite is noise until this one passes: if the allowed case is refused, the policy is not discriminating, it is just closed.

cases.title: a host nobody allowed
cases.notes: The whole point of the allow-list. If nothing else here runs, this one must.

cases.title: credentials in the URL
cases.notes: Refused before the host is even considered, in all three. They would be sent to whatever host the rest of the string names, and a model that can compose a URL can compose that.

cases.title: plain http against an https policy
cases.notes: Ordering matters and is pinned by url-0005: scheme is checked before the private-address test, so a plain-http loopback URL reports the scheme, not the address.

cases.title: the cloud metadata endpoint, explicitly allow-listed
cases.notes: THE row that matters most in this suite. Every language refuses it, and 169.254.169.254 is the single most valuable target an SSRF can reach — tested in its ALLOW-LISTED form on purpose, because an operator naming it explicitly is exactly the mistake the policy has to survive. All three now say `private_address_refused`. The reference used to say `private_network_refused`, so a consumer switching on the code fell through to its default branch in one of the two directions and read an SSRF refusal as an unknown failure; closed by the reference adopting the ports name and accessor. See G-21.

cases.title: loopback, explicitly allow-listed
cases.notes: Second address family, same refusal. Pinned separately from url-0005 because a fix that special-cased link-local would turn that row green and leave this one red. Loopback is how an attacker reaches every service on the host that assumed it was unreachable, and allow-listing it does not make it public.

cases.title: an RFC 1918 address, explicitly allow-listed
cases.notes: Third address family, and the row that makes this trio a per-ADDRESS claim rather than a per-network one — which is why the reference took the ports spelling rather than the other way round. Together with url-0005 and url-0006 it pins that the behaviour is identical in all three, so G-21 was always a rename and never a hole.

cases.title: a port nobody allowed
cases.notes: Checked AFTER the host, in all three. A URL that fails both reports the host, which is the more useful of the two to a reader.

cases.title: not a URL at all
cases.notes: A parser that accepted this would hand a relative string to an engine and let it resolve against whatever page is currently open.

cases.title: a relative path
cases.notes: The realistic shape of the same mistake. A model asked to 'go to the admin page' composes exactly this.

cases.title: a trailing dot and mixed case in the host
cases.notes: `docs.example.com.` is the same origin as `docs.example.com`, and a policy that missed the equivalence would be trivially bypassed in the other direction — an attacker-supplied host that the allow-list fails to match is safe, but one the allow-list fails to RECOGNISE as already-allowed teaches operators to widen it.

cases.title: a public host that merely contains an allowed one
cases.notes: The suffix attack. A `str_contains` or `endsWith` implementation of the allow-list passes this and hands the agent to an attacker-controlled origin; every implementation here compares the whole label.
